sections.text: A business loan is judged on two numbers: whether your income covers the payment, and what the money really costs once fees and the term are included. The first is the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), which is monthly net operating income divided by the monthly loan payment. On a $180,000 loan at an assumed 9.5% with $6,500 of monthly operating income, DSCR is 0.41 over 12 months, 1.13 over 36 months and 1.72 over 60 months. The same business and the same loan look unaffordable or comfortable depending only on the term.
DSCR: what it measures and how to use it

DSCR = monthly net operating income / monthly loan payment. A ratio of 1.00 means income exactly covers the payment; 1.25 means $1.25 of income for every $1.00 owed. The Business Loan Calculator labels a result of 1.5 or more as strong, 1.25 to 1.5 as good, 1.0 to 1.25 as marginal and below 1.0 as insufficient. Those bands are a screening guide, not a published lender requirement. Lenders define operating income in their own ways, may count your other debt payments too, and set their own minimums, so ask any lender for its definition and threshold. The SBA publishes the rules for its own programs on sba.gov, and they change, so check there rather than relying on a figure in an article.

items: Loan $180,000 at 9.5% a year, fixed, with equal monthly payments. The rate is an assumption for illustration, not a quote for any loan type.
Monthly net operating income $6,500, treated as steady. No other debt payments.
Interest is charged monthly at one-twelfth of the annual rate. Origination fees are zero in this table and added in the next one.

sections.text: A longer term raises DSCR and makes the loan easier to qualify for, but total interest climbs. Moving from 60 to 84 months lowers the payment by $838.42 and adds $20,300.90 of interest. At these numbers, the shortest term that reaches a DSCR of 1.25 is 41 months, and 1.5 needs 51 months. Choosing the term is a trade-off between approval, cash flow and total cost, and it should also match how long the financed asset will be useful.
How much could this business borrow?

Reverse the same logic to find a borrowing limit. With $6,500 of income, a lender who wants 1.25 would allow a payment of up to $5,200 ($6,500 divided by 1.25). At 9.5% that supports a loan of about $247,597 over 60 months, or $318,160 over 84 months. At a target of 1.5, the payment cap is $4,333.33, supporting about $206,331 over 60 months. If the business already has $800 a month in other debt service, DSCR on the $180,000, 60-month loan falls from 1.72 to 1.42.

An origination fee is usually deducted from the loan, so you receive less than you borrow but repay the full amount. The effective annual rate on the cash you actually receive is higher than the stated rate. On this loan over 60 months, a 2% fee raises the effective rate from 9.50% to 10.37%, a 3% fee to 10.82% and a 5% fee to 11.73%. The same 3% fee costs more per year the shorter the loan:

Effective rates here come from solving for the rate at which the payments equal the cash received, the same approach used in the APR calculation. Compare lenders on that effective rate and on total dollars repaid, because a lender with a lower stated rate and a larger fee can cost more.

items: Compute your DSCR at several terms and see which one clears the threshold you expect.
Get written quotes that show the rate, every fee, the term and any prepayment charge.
Ask whether a personal guarantee or collateral is required, and what happens if the business cannot pay.
Match the term to the asset. Financing equipment that lasts 5 years over 10 leaves you paying for it after it is gone.
Check whether the loan can be repaid early without a penalty.

sections.text: When this analysis does not apply

The table assumes fixed rates, level payments and steady income. Variable rates, balloon payments, lines of credit, seasonal income, and revenue-based repayment work differently. Income that varies by month can make an average DSCR misleading, so look at your weakest months too. Treat these figures as illustrations, not an offer or advice. Enter your own amount, term, rate, fee and income into the Business Loan Calculator, then confirm every number against the lender's disclosure.
